title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but it was unknown whether pharmacologic lowering of Lp(a) reduces cardiovascular events. Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide directed at hepatic apolipoprotein(a) synthesis. Lp(a)HORIZON (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04023552) was designed to test the Lp(a) hypothesis in secondary prevention. METHODS: Lp(a)HORIZON was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial conducted at 797 sites in 42 countries. Eligible patients had established cardiovascular disease, with a qualifying cardiovascular event between 3 months and 10 years before enrollment, and a baseline Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL (approximately 148 nmol/L). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to pelacarsen 80 mg administered subcutaneously once monthly or to matching placebo administered on the same schedule, on a background of guideline-directed therapy. Randomization was stratified by screening Lp(a) level so as to balance patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (approximately 192 nmol/L), who constituted a prespecified second primary analysis population. The primary endpoint was expanded major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE): a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and urgent coronary revascularization. A total of 8,350 patients were randomly assigned and 8,322 were included in the efficacy analysis. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 4.7 years, the primary expanded-MACE endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients assigned to pelacarsen and in 12.1% of patients assigned to placebo (hazard ratio, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.90 to 1.15). The exact P value for the primary comparison could not be verified in the available secondary sources and is therefore not reported here. The neutral result was consistent across the individual components of the composite. In the prespecified population with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL, the primary endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients in each group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15). Pelacarsen had the expected biologic effect on its target: Lp(a) was reduced by 78.4% at 12 months, with a median Lp(a) at 12 months of 64.4 nmol/L with pelacarsen versus 233.4 nmol/L with placebo. Reported safety and tolerability details beyond the above (including rates of study-drug discontinuation, which were reported as higher with pelacarsen) could not be confirmed by two independent sources and are not reported here. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with established cardiovascular disease and an Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL, pelacarsen 80 mg subcutaneously once monthly lowered Lp(a) by approximately 78% but did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events as compared with placebo over a median of 4.7 years. The investigators have stated that the findings were unexpected and disappointing and that they apply specifically to pelacarsen in a secondary-prevention setting, rather than invalidating Lp(a) as a causal risk factor.

title: Long-Term Impact of Vutrisiran in Patients With TTR Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy: 1-Year Efficacy and Safety Outcomes From the HELIOS-B Open-Label Extension
abstract: BACKGROUND: In HELIOS-B (A Study to Evaluate Vutrisiran in Patients With Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy), vutrisiran reduced the risk of all-cause mortality (ACM) and recurrent cardiovascular events and slowed disease progression measures versus placebo in patients with TTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy after 33 to 36 months. We report the long-term efficacy and safety of vutrisiran from an ongoing open-label extension of HELIOS-B. METHODS: Patients who completed HELIOS-B could enroll in the open-label extension, continuing with vutrisiran 25 mg every 3 months (continuous vutrisiran) or, if previously receiving placebo, initiating vutrisiran 25 mg every 3 months (placebo/vutrisiran). Prespecified end points assessed in the open-label extension are the composite of ACM and cardiovascular events, ACM, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary score, New York Heart Association class, and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) and troponin I levels. Outcomes were assessed through month 48 in this analysis. RESULTS: Of 654 participants in HELIOS-B (vutrisiran, n=326; placebo, n=328), 478 completed double-blind treatment and 466 (vutrisiran, n=243; placebo, n=223) entered the open-label extension. In the continuous vutrisiran group, the risk of first cardiovascular event or ACM was reduced by 37% (hazard ratio, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.51, 0.79]; P=0.0001) and ACM by 37% (hazard ratio, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.46, 0.84]; P=0.0023) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Through month 48, patients in the continuous vutrisiran group had preserved health status and quality of life per Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary score (least squares mean difference, 9.0 [95% CI, 5.3, 12.6]; P<0.0001) and more patients had improved or stable New York Heart Association class (odds ratio, 1.6 [95% CI, 1.1, 2.2]; P=0.0084) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Benefits in the continuous vutrisiran group were maintained for NT-proBNP and troponin I levels (adjusted geometric mean fold change ratios, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.58, 0.74]; P<0.0001; and 0.71 [95% CI, 0.64, 0.79]; P<0.0001, respectively) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Similar benefits were observed in the vutrisiran monotherapy population. No new safety signals were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Long-term vutrisiran resulted in clinically meaningful benefits across mortality, cardiovascular events, cardiac biomarkers, functional status, and quality of life in patients with TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy through month 48. Patients initially treated with vutrisiran had better outcomes than those first receiving placebo, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and treatment in TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04153149.

title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
abstract: BACKGROUND: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population. RESULTS: A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).

title: The Impact of Clinical and Biochemical Frailty on Outcomes following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty results from declining reserve and function and is a modifiable cardiovascular risk-factor. Despite this, there is limited evidence surrounding its role in lower-risk TAVR cohorts. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate frailty among contemporary TAVR patients, delineate the impact of biochemical and clinical frailty, and understand its additive value to existing risk-prediction tools. METHODS: Analysis of a multicenter Australian registry. Biochemical frailty (BF) was defined as serum albumin <35 g/L and clinical frailty (CF) as a Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale ≥5. Patients meeting BF or CF criteria were categorized as frail. RESULTS: Of the 2,661 patients, the median age 82 (IQR: 77-86), 60% male, and median STS 3.3 (2-5.2), 920 patients (35%) were considered frail. A total of 171 (19%) of frail patients fulfilled both BF and CF criteria. The frail group was older (83 vs 81, P < 0.001), more females (43% vs 38%; P = 0.016) with higher STS scores (4 vs 3, P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed a stepwise increase in 12-month mortality with increasing frailty (no frailty 4% vs BF or CF 7% vs BF + CF 16%, Log-rank P < 0.001). In Cox proportional hazards regression BF or CF (adjusted HR: 1.6; 95% CI: 1.0-2.4; P = 0.033) and BF + CF (adjusted HR: 3.3; 95% CI: 1.9-5.6; P < 0.001) independently predicted 12-month mortality. Addition of frailty to STS Score improved mortality prediction (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve: 0.608 vs 0.664; DeLong's P = 0.021), with Shapley analysis demonstrating significant contribution from frailty. CONCLUSIONS: Frailty is common with significant implications in TAVR. Patients with biochemical and clinical frailty criteria are highest risk. Development of strategies to address frailty is critical.

title: Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in transcatheter mitral interventions: percutaneous anterior leaflet modification
abstract: Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) remains one of the most catastrophic complications of transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) interventions, including TMVR in native valve, valve-in-valve, valve-in-ring, and valve-in-mitral annular calcification procedures. Its incidence varies widely across procedural types (0%-40%), with mortality rates approaching 36%, and represents a leading cause of patient ineligibility, excluding 4%-50% of candidates from TMVR. Accurate pre-procedural risk stratification relies on cardiac computed tomography, which enables annular sizing, virtual valve implantation, neo- and skirt neo-left ventricular outflow tract area quantification, and fluoroscopic projection planning. Key anatomic determinants of LVOTO include anterior mitral leaflet length, aortomitral angle, septal hypertrophy, left ventricular cavity size, and device-related factors. To mitigate LVOTO risk and expand treatment eligibility, in addition to septal modification, anterior mitral leaflet modification techniques have emerged, broadly categorized into electrosurgical laceration approaches-LAMPOON and ELASTA-and balloon-assisted translocation techniques for balloon-expandable valves-BATMAN, CLEVE, DETROIT, and ROBIN. Each strategy addresses distinct anatomic substrates and procedural scenarios, and their complementary profiles support individualized technique selection. This review aims to present an in-depth discussion of LVOTO in TMVR and anterior leaflet modification strategies.

title: Characteristics and Thresholds of Coronary Lesions to Predict Acute Coronary Syndrome From Artificial Intelligence-Guided Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography
abstract: BACKGROUND: Characteristics of future culprit lesions according to artificial intelligence-guided quantitative computed tomography (AI-QCT) are unknown. OBJECTIVES: The authors aimed to characterize and derive thresholds to predict future culprit lesions from coronary computed tomography angiography using AI-QCT. METHODS: A total of 2,169 patients/13,772 lesions undergoing coronary computed tomography angiography at Turku University Hospital, Finland, (derivation) and 553 patients/3,948 lesions from Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands, (validation) were analyzed with AI-QCT. Lesions from vessels undergoing early revascularization were excluded. Lesion-level total plaque volume (TPV) and noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV) thresholds were derived and externally validated to predict lesion-level and patient-level acute coronary syndrome (ACS). RESULTS: Future culprit lesions from both cohorts (n = 69 validation; n = 15 derivation) had consistently higher median TPV (101 mm3 validation; 115 mm3 derivation; P = 0.811) and NCPV (65 mm3 validation; 74 mm3 derivation; P = 0.709) compared with control lesions (P < 0.001) and were nonobstructive in 69.6% (derivation) and 40.0% (validation). Thresholds of TPV ≥55 mm3 and NCPV ≥32 mm3 were derived and associated with significantly higher adjusted rates of lesion-level (TPV ≥55 mm3: adjusted HR: 12.09; 95% CI: 6.95-21.04; P < 0.001; NCPV ≥32 mm3: adjusted HR: 10.82; 95% CI: 6.22-18.80; P < 0.001) and patient-level ACS (TPV ≥55 mm3: adjusted HR: 2.92; 95% CI: 1.65-5.16; P < 0.001; NCPV ≥32 mm3: adjusted HR: 5.11; 95% CI: 2.49-10.46; P < 0.001) with consistent results in the validation cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Future culprit lesions vs nonculprit lesions by AI-QCT demonstrated significantly higher plaque volumes and were nonobstructive in 40% to 70%. Thresholds of TPV ≥55 mm3 and NCPV ≥32 mm3 were derived to predict future culprit lesions and associated with increased rates of lesion-level and patient-level ACS in 2 independent cohorts.

title: Prevalence of Angiographic Coronary Artery Disease in Systolic Heart Failure Without Infarct-Pattern Late Gadolinium Enhancement: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
abstract: AIMS: Rest late gadolinium enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR) identifies infarct-pattern scar but does not assess coronary anatomy. We estimated the prevalence of angiographic coronary artery disease (CAD) among adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) or otherwise unexplained left ventricular systolic dysfunction without infarct-pattern LGE. METHODS AND RESULTS: MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched to 27 July 2026. Eligible studies provided separable scar-negative denominators and corresponding angiographic CAD counts from invasive coronary angiography (ICA). Scar-negative was defined as the absence of subendocardial or transmural LGE in a coronary distribution. Random-effects logit meta-analysis used restricted maximum likelihood and Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Twenty-two reports representing 20 studies included 2,236 paired LGE-CMR and ICA. 818 patients had infarct-pattern scar, and 1,418 were scar-negative. Eight studies contributed 44 CAD cases among 468 scar-negative patients for ≥50% stenosis, giving a pooled prevalence of 10.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 7.4-15.4). Five studies contributed 19 CAD cases among 271 scar-negative patients for ≥70% stenosis, giving a pooled prevalence of 7.6% (95% CI 4.4-12.6). Seven studies contributed 33 CAD cases among 679 scar-negative patients for high-risk-pattern CAD, giving a pooled prevalence of 4.9% (95% CI 2.2-10.6) and a 95% prediction interval of 0.8-24.8%. These strata represented different study subsets and were not nested. CONCLUSION: Among selected adults with HFrEF or otherwise unexplained LVSD who underwent paired LGE-CMR and ICA, absence of infarct-pattern LGE did not exclude angiographic CAD. Further coronary assessment should be considered when resolving that uncertainty would alter diagnosis or management.

title: Long-term outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents versus coronary artery bypass grafting for left main coronary artery disease: a prospective analysis of the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry
abstract: BACKGROUND: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents has been widely used to treat patients with left main coronary artery disease; however, long-term comparative outcomes versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in real-world populations remain poorly characterised. We aimed to compare long-term all-cause mortality after PCI or CABG in Asian patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease. METHODS: We analysed prospectively collected data from the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry, conducted at 46 hospitals in South Korea, India, Japan, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The registry enrolled adults aged 18 years or older with unprotected left main coronary artery disease (defined as a stenosis diameter of ≥50% as visually estimated on angiography), who had been treated with PCI, CABG, or medical therapy alone. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used a target trial emulation framework to compare the long-term risk of all-cause mortality between PCI with drug-eluting stents and isolated CABG. We used propensity-score overlap weighting to adjust for measured baseline covariates. The IRIS-MAIN Registry study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01341327). FINDINGS: Between Jan 1, 2003, and Dec 31, 2024, 6900 patients were enrolled in the IRIS-MAIN registry, of whom 5379 (78·0%) underwent coronary revascularisation through either PCI with drug-eluting stents (3836 [71·3%]) or CABG (1543 [28·7%]) and were included in the analysis. The median duration of follow-up for all patients was 10·0 years (IQR 5·0-16·7). In the overlap-weighted population, no statistically detectable difference in 10-year weighted Kaplan-Meier rates of all-cause mortality was observed between PCI and CABG (24·0% vs 22·9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1·00 [95% CI 0·87-1·14]; p=0·99). The confidence interval does not exclude a mortality benefit or harm with either strategy. INTERPRETATION: In this non-randomised registry analysis of patients with left main coronary artery disease, there was no statistically detectable difference in all-cause mortality between PCI and CABG. For patients considered suitable for either strategy, multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion might help patients and clinicians weigh potential trade-offs in the choice between PCI and CABG. These findings are observational and cannot establish causal treatment effects or equivalence in survival. FUNDING: The CardioVascular Research Foundation (South Korea).
